utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you all. It's been such a long time, some of the faces. It's good to see them back. The Chamber was concerned to hear of the illness of Mr. Vasic, Mr. Domazet, and we did extend, through officers, our good wishes to him. We hope that he is proceeding with recovery. Mr. Moore, there is a change of counsel appearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. We've got the good fortune of having Mr. Vincent Lunny, who comes from Scotland originally, and he will be assisting us in our case as Mr. Smith has gone on to greater fields.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. We welcome Mr. Lunny. Now, the purpose of the session this afternoon is to deal with issues before we commence the evidence in the Defence in this case. There are a number of issues that are apparent at this stage, and we propose to go through them. Before we do so, could I ask, first of you, Mr. Moore, whether there is any particular issue that the Prosecution would want to raise at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there isn't anything that immediately stands out. There are topics which clearly will require decisions from the Trial Chamber. There is one area perhaps in relation to whether certain summaries are adequate or not, but that may be dependent upon other rulings. The only other matters that I would be concerned about are the level of notice that the Prosecution should receive from the Defence in respect of witnesses to be called. We would submit that the same principle of two days' notice should apply. And indeed we would submit that all the criteria that were used for the Prosecution by way of service of documentation should also apply in relation to the Defence presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As matters stand, just to assist the Court, we had information that on Friday, that the first witness to be called by the Defence, that the summons had not been served as of Friday. We do not know what the situation might be. I put that forward to assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Now, Mr. Domazet, first, would you be able to indicate your understanding of the present position concerning Mr. Vasic's health?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all. Mr. Vasic underwent his last examination, as predicted, on the 24th of this month. He has now started to work with us again. He's working on our witnesses in Belgrade and making the necessary preparations for our case to begin. If everything goes fine, he expects to be in The Hague this coming Friday. Therefore, I hope that he will be joining us here in this courtroom as of next Monday. His health will certainly be a problem. When he is here, I expect he will be able to give you a much more thorough update on the state of his health. Despite the fact that he had been advised by his doctors to desist from working until at least the end of September and spend the entire month recovering, he decided to start work. He is able to resume his normal activities to some extent, but he tires easily. One thing that he asked me - and I believe this can be raised later, when scheduling is discussed - he would certainly like to take an active part in the proceedings. He does believe, however, that five days a week would be too strenuous a pace for him throughout the Mrksic Defence case. He believes that one day off per week, be it Friday or any other day, would be much more conducive to his appearances in the court-room. Needless to say, I wish him every luck and I would like him to continue as lead counsel. I am a mere co-counsel, and I joined the trial two or three days late. I do not think I would be in a position to be in charge of the Defence case without him; however, as things are at the moment, I believe he will be joining us despite all the difficulty, for which I apologise to both the Trial Chamber and to the OTP. I am here referring to the number of delays that were caused by all of our problems. We have provided a witness list for our case, but this I believe is a matter which will be discussed later, since Your Honour's question was only about Mr. Vasic's health. Therefore, I expect that all these issues raised by Mr. Moore about the witnesses will be raised at some point. We have provided our first list, and I expect that we shall be submitting a continuation of that over the following days, today and possibly tomorrow, however, we have experienced a great deal of difficulty for all the above-mentioned reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just intervene for one moment, because you did ask a question how things were and I wanted to hear how the case of Mrksic was going to deal with certain problems. Could I ask the Court to have a look at a document that I've had prepared for my learned friends and the Court. It really relates to what I will call the witness situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that is being distributed, Mr. Moore --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And there's three for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- yes, I propose first to ask Mr. Borovic whether there is any particular matter which the Defence of Mr. Radic would like to raise. We will be dealing with the ordinary issues, but we want to make sure that we hear you if there's some particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to welcome you, too, back to this case after our break. I hope our cooperation will be as great as before the break. As for the witnesses, we will be speaking about that later, but there are two principal issues that perhaps we should raise today. As regards the witness list in this case -- or rather, a particular witness, I am talking about a note that was submitted at a later stage pursuant to an order from the Chamber, as regards that note, the ruling is that it should be submitted, that is the original text, to all the Defence teams, that a handwriting expert should be called in to judge the authenticity of that note. And all we can say is that we will not be going into any further detail until all of these actions are taken. On the other hand, I do believe that the OTP's submission is groundless, that only some aspects are legally relevant. If anything at all is tendered, then we seek that the entire note be tendered because we lost countless hours examining the witness about a whole series of circumstances concerning that note. He did confirm some of our submissions. When we checked the photocopy of this note, we realised that many of the things that the witness said before this Trial Chamber were just simply not true. We were adamant about that note because we had misgivings about the authenticity of certain portions of that note, or maybe the entire note. We believe the Trial Chamber should accept that. If the entire note is admitted into evidence, then we would move that further cross-examination of this witness be allowed; namely, the Radic Defence believes that this would be in the best interests of an equitable approach. This was the last witness. The Prosecution left him as the last witness to testify to some aspects of my client's responsibility. My remarks are about all these circumstances that I have now spoken about. Additionally, if all of these proposals are accepted by the Trial Chamber, including some of the OTP proposals, then the Defence would be adamant that we be allowed another chance to additionally cross-examine this witness. Another issue, Your Honour, by your leave, it's about the OTP's contacts with Defence witnesses. On the 11th of July, 2006, we submitted a 65 ter list motion, after which, in compliance with the orders, we also filed supplements to some of the summaries. I think this is something that can be raised later in the course of today's hearing. As for the witnesses, all of them are mentioned on our 65 ter list. The OTP asked that the Trial Chamber allow, in keeping with Article 18 of the Statute and Rule 39(I) of the Rules, new interviews be conducted with these witnesses from the Defence 65 ter list. The motion was filed on the 17th of August, but on the 3rd of August, which means a great deal earlier, the witnesses received their summons. Police officers came to their flats to serve these on them, saying that they were witnesses to some circumstances and events that occurred in the former Yugoslavia. The summons remained unspecified as well as the events and circumstances. It is our belief that although we do not fear whatever it is that these witnesses might say to the OTP, this is a move which might lead to these witnesses being intimidated. Everything the OTP might want to know can be found out in cross-examination, and Rule 39(E) refers to the pre-trial stage when evidence is gathered, and not something like this. These are some matters of principle that we felt the Chamber ought to know about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Could I mention that for the most part they are the subject of motions presently before the Chamber for decision. If it is that you want either additional material or you want to put new submissions to the Chamber, that should be done immediately because decisions will be coming out this week in respect of those matters. So I could urge you to deal with that as soon as possible, if that is your position. And of course, if something new emerges from decision, you will be in a position to move some further motion and advance it and support it in the normal way. Thank you. Mr. Lukic, is there any particular matter which concerns the Sljivancanin Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I assume that you will be asking questions today about all the things that we are here for. There is one thing I'd like to say about my friend Mr. Borovic's position in as far as my understanding of your position in relation to these two motions are concerned that have been dealt with. There is another argument in addition to what we wrote in our written motion regarding the Prosecutor's motion to interview witnesses. I would ask the Chamber to please take this additional argument into account, in addition to all the other arguments in our written motion. Mr. Borovic spoke about this a while ago, but I would say that this is a procedural argument. The Prosecutor now wishes to interview our witnesses; this is long after the 65 ter motion had been filed and we're well into our proceedings. We all agreed in this court-room, both the Prosecutor and the Defence teams, that both the Statute and the Rules say nothing about this sort of motion. There are no definite rules governing such cases. We decided to all rely on the jurisprudence of the Tribunal as known up to this point. There is one thing I'd like to say, though. Article 18 of the Statute and Rule 39 of the Rules address the possibility of having additional interviews with witnesses, but this is only about the investigation stage. Article 18 is under the heading "Investigations" and so is Rule 39 of the Rules. My interpretation is that whoever wrote the Statute and the Rules allowed for this possibility to occur while evidence is gathered for the OTP case, and at that stage alone. Yet, the OTP now wish to re-interview certain witnesses, but we don't know which witnesses exactly. After they have concluded their case, it is for this reason that I believe the Prosecutor should, under the Statute and the Rules, not be allowed to re-interview these witnesses. If it's for the purposes of new evidence, then that would be all right; or, for example, if a witness like Florence Hartmann appears, this is something new for their case, but they can't interview witnesses now once their case has been concluded and once they have led all their evidence without this being in relation to possible later evidence emerging from the Defence case. Everything else is the same as before. We shall try not to repeat ourselves, but if you want us to further elucidate our position, we are prepared to, needless to say. As for everything else, I fully agree with what Mr. Borovic said in relation to that document. I believe sufficient detail has been provided about this. I would merely add that in relation to such documents, this Trial Chamber, at least, has taken a very clear-cut position. When those diaries emerged, we could not get acquainted with those before the witness appeared; on the other hand, when additional documents appeared in relation to certain witnesses, the witnesses were then re-examined or re-appeared for cross-examination. I don't think the Trial Chamber would be facing any sort of a dilemma were it not the case that the Prosecutor has already concluded their case. Things being what they are, it's down to the Chamber to rule on this and decide which course of action should be taken. So far so good. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. We will proceed now to look at matters that appear to require attention under the existing Rule 65 ter and Rule 73 ter. Now, in that respect, the Trial Chamber at a Pre-Defence Conference has the power to set the number of witnesses that will be called by each Defence team and determine the time allocated to the Defence to present its case. Could I indicate that in respect of each of those, we would defer our action and decision. And as this conference continues, you will understand why. But we formally defer, and we may return to that at some near time in the future. There have been issues raised concerning the adequacy of the summaries that have been provided by the Defence. And I think, Mr. Moore, that brings us perhaps to the sheet of paper or papers that you've had distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to take them slightly out of order, if I may. May I go to the case for Sljivancanin. One can see quite clearly there's 24 witnesses, and -- or we can see with the exception of witness 24, Mr. Sljivancanin, the summaries that have been received are now adequate. My learned friend amended his original summaries, and that meets our requirements. With regard to the Radic witnesses at the very start, rather there are, in reality, seven witnesses. Witness 1 and 3 -- because this has been subject to various motions. The Court is aware there have been a large number of motions moving backward and forward. Witness 1 and Witness 3 we initially took the view that the summaries were adequate. In actual fact, I take the view they are inadequate, and we would ask my learned friend - who has shown willing so far - to additionally add the summaries on Witness 1 and 3. The rest are perfectly acceptable. So Witness 1 and Witness 3 we would ask for expanded summaries, and the rest, they are fine. In relation to Mr. Radic, he falls into a slightly different category. Initially he was not going to be a witness. An application has been made for him to be called. I can say now we do not oppose that; however, the summary that we have received is inadequate and we would ask for that to be expanded. But that has been much more recent and it may be a question of time. May I now, then, deal with the matter that concerns us the most, which are the witnesses for Mr. Mrksic. Your Honours can see that there are 36. If we exclude Witness 12, 13, 24, and then 33 to 35 inclusive, I regret to say that the adequacy of the summaries, it demonstrates that they are wholly inadequate. As often as not we are getting references to five hours in chief, but the summary might be six lines or eight lines. The Rules are quite specific about the summaries. They are summaries, we accept that, but it's not a case of topics; it's a question of facts that the Defence seek to rely upon. And in this case, we say the Defence have failed comprehensively. So we would seek an order for those summaries to be expanded and to conform with the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, the first five witnesses you contend at the moment that you don't yet have adequate summaries. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is Your Honour referring to the witnesses for Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The sequence, as I understand it, is witness 33 is witness 1. Witness 14 should be number 2. Witness 31 there is or are queries in relation to it. It's not fatal, I don't pretend that it's fatal, but it certainly is required. Witness 4 and 5 are adequate. So that will get us over the first hurdle in relation to time with the -- the first witness having a query on it, the matter that I've already referred the Court to. So we would be able to proceed with those witnesses. However, may I just indicate the problem that may arise, and it is quite simply this, that without adequate summaries from other witnesses, we do not know whether the questions that we would seek to ask witnesses 1 to 5 inclusive are really 2 to 5 inclusive are going to deal with all the topics that may arise subsequently. And clearly, the Rules are created to give cross-examining party, whether it be Defence or Prosecution, an element of notice of topics that may be raised in the -- in that case. Because we have the inadequacy, we are unable to say whether in actual fact the cross-examination that we will do will fully meet the topics that may arise subsequently. That clearly is the reason for the Rule. We would submit that even though my learned friend Mr. Vasic has been ill, the case of Mrksic at one stage was going to commence before the break, and they surely must have proofs of evidence or some indication of what topics they will be dealing with as well as the facts, because it is the facts for which these witnesses are silent. So we seek an order for my learned friend, who is an experienced co-counsel and has had two months to prepare this, to please now furnish those details as a matter of expedition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, is it not the order of the Chamber that these matters after the first five witnesses be provided by Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I believe that is the order, but my understanding was from the way my learned friend was speaking that there was going to be considerable difficulty in relation to that and that they may not be able to adhere to the order of the Court. That's -- that is the worry that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the proposition you've been advancing is that what has been provided so far is inadequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber, by its order, has accepted that for all but one witness and has -- there is an order on foot for it, a matter to be remedied by next Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, then I will leave the matter there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Domazet, is there anything you wish to say or add?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the way I understand Mr. Moore's words -- as for these first five witnesses, there seem to be no problems for the OTP. It seems that the only objections being raised and -- are in relation to two witnesses, as in not being very adequate. We are talking about witness number 14 and witness number 31. I will have a look, and I don't think that should be too much trouble to deal with. The remaining witnesses in the OTP's submission are sufficiently documented. As for all these other witnesses, I have been told to submit by this coming Friday a more detailed statement of reasons. It's true, I did say it would be difficult to get this done by Friday, and I would ask, if possible, for this deadline to be extended until sometime next week. Because, as I stated at the outset, I will be expecting Mr. Vasic here in The Hague on Friday evening. I will be going through all of this with him over the weekend and try to complete this task. The reason being, he was the person who previously worked with me on this first part, and he is the person who has been in touch with our witnesses earlier, as now. All the more so because I expect that in relation to some of the witnesses we shall withdraw -- or rather, we shall withdraw some of our witnesses from the list. Some were impossible to get in touch with, some simply refused. I do have to see Mr. Vasic, talk to him about it, and see what the state of these matters is. I don't think I could do this adequately or as the OTP expect me to by Friday. As far as information in relation to these two remaining witnesses is concerned, I could elaborate on that, and then the first five would be okay by the OTP. I would ask that my deadline be moved to sometime next week, Tuesday possibly, because I would try to use the weekend to work with Mr. Vasic on this and eventually complete this task. The same thing applies to personal details. Unfortunately, we have not been able to submit these in relation to some witnesses. We are in the process of receiving the personal details of some witnesses. I have two new witnesses now. This evening I'll be receiving some more, probably. We have already started submitting these to the OTP as we are receiving them, and we shall continue in that fashion. This has nothing to do with the motion. We shall keep submitting this sort of information to the OTP on a daily basis. I believe that I have answered your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the view of the Chamber, Mr. Domazet, and in view of the very particular circumstances that exist, we would vary the order presently made in respect of the provision of summaries of the evidence to be provided by each witness to be called by the Mrksic Defence so that the additional details sought in respect of witnesses 14 and 31 be provided immediately. The summaries of the next five witnesses, that is witnesses 6 to 10, to be called by the Mrksic Defence to be provided by Friday of this week. The summaries of the remainder of the witnesses to be provided by Wednesday of next week. And by those means, we hope that we will make provisions sufficient to enable the difficulties concerning Mr. Domazet to be overcome. Now, Mr. Borovic, Mr. Moore mentioned three witnesses on your list, 1, 3, and 8, with the note that they needed amplification. Is that something you accept should be attended to? Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. I will be dealing with this issue that you just put, Your Honours, to the Defence of Miroslav Radic. OTP in their submissions required additional information -- or rather, they wanted the summaries for all witnesses proposed by Radic's Defence to be extended. On the 31st we provided additional summaries, on the 31st of July. These summaries pertain to three witnesses, whereas the remaining two witnesses were outstanding until we received the ruling of the Trial Chamber as to which type of defence was to be used and whether there was any room for the use of the defence of alibi under Rule 67. We received the ruling of the Trial Chamber, and I will give you the date presently. It was dated the 22nd of July. And in paragraph 8 of that ruling it is stated that the OTP informed informally the Trial Chamber that it was content with these summaries and that this problem was not going to be raised again. The Defence acted in accordance with the Chamber's ruling dated the 22nd of August and supplied the addendum for two witnesses that the OTP required. Therefore, I have to say that we're quite surprised to hear now at the Pre-Defence Conference that the OTP is once again dissatisfied with the summaries provided for witnesses 3 and 1. As for witness number 8, what the OTP said is quite correct and we shall definitely supplement the summary. The reason for this summary being somewhat short is that we ran out of time, and we wanted to wait until the accused Radic received the status of the witness. As for witnesses 1 and 3, it is quite clear that they will be testifying about a very narrow issue. In our summaries, we stated everything that could be potentially relevant and useful to the OTP. We are unable to put in absolutely all of the evidence in the summary. The OTP will be able to explore this further when preparing for their cross-examination. It is simply impossible for us to add any other information to the summaries that have already been supplemented, because based on the existing summaries it is quite clear that these witnesses will be testifying about a very narrow issue, both geographically and temporally. It pertains to just one item in the indictment, thus we fear that the Defence is unable to provide any supplemental information. As for witness number 8, we will supplement the summary as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore, witnesses 1 and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We just wish to have clarification on really it is one paragraph in a summary and another paragraph. We are not making a significant complaint in any way at all. I'm quite sure it can be done with discussion with my learned friends informally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will leave it on that basis, Mr. Moore, for witnesses 1 and 3. Quite clearly what has been provided in respect of the accused Mr. Radic requires to be substantially developed. There can be no question of that. Very well. And Mr. Lukic gets a good housekeeping seal of approval. Try and keep it up, Mr. Lukic. Yes. There was mention in the witness lists of the possibilities of witnesses being provided or dealt with by way of a statement under 92 bis by one or two of the Defences, not all of them. And there has been a suggestion also that there might be evidence taken under Rule 73 -- 71. With respect to 92 bis, the Chamber would indicate that if parties intend to use 92 bis, it would be beneficial for everybody for planning if those applications were made shortly. With respect to Rule 71, if that is to be -- if that is still under consideration, the Chamber would like to suggest that it can see no practical advantage at this stage in this trial of deposition evidence under Rule 71. If the subject matter is amenable to Rule 92 bis, that would be more practical. If, as is apparent, though, the use of Rule 71 doesn't save any time because counsel need to be present when the deposition is taken, to cross-examine. So that we would have to adjourn here to allow evidence to be taken wherever the witness was. So we're losing time. If there's a problem about the witness travelling because of health or some such, look at 92 bis or look at the idea of a videolink to overcome the difficulty of travel. So could we suggest that thought be given to those other possibilities. It's not a matter of excluding the evidence, it's a matter of finding the most efficient way of receiving it, and we would suggest that, unless there's something we're unaware of, Rule 71 wouldn't appear to save anybody any time or add to the efficiency of what's intended. Expert reports. We understand that each Defence intends to lead expert evidence. There is clearly advantage in due notice of that being given. And then there is a requirement, of course, that the Chamber fix times for that to be done and for the Prosecution to respond to each expert report. We would have in mind, given the course of evidence that will be proceeding, that the -- Monday, the 18th of September, should be the date fixed for the filing and disclosure of expert reports and that the Prosecution should respond in respect of the expert report of the accused Radic and Sljivancanin by Monday, the 16th of October. In respect of the expert report of the accused Mrksic, one week earlier; that is, the 9th of October. If I could return to Rule 92 bis statements, it would seem useful if we indicate that the two Defences contemplating 92 bis witnesses should have an indication of a time. I forgot to deal with this when I mentioned them a little while ago. We would suggest again Monday, the 25th of September, for any motions for 92 bis. That's four weeks from now, which should be adequate time for those to be looked at. One witness being considered by the Mrksic Defence, Mr. Domazet, is Mrs. Mrksic, and it's mentioned that she might give evidence partly under 92 bis and partly by oral testimony. Could we suggest a way of simplifying this for you. 92 bis is a fairly complex procedure. If Mrs. Mrksic is to attend to give some evidence, you could use Rule 89(F) to provide simply a statement of the parts that are not covered in your intentions. She could attend to give her evidence and simply tender the statement, affirming it to be correct, and then go on to deal with those parts of the evidence that you want to be dealt with by oral testimony, and in that way diminishing your pre-trial preparation and your preparation and the work that has to be done away from here, but not lengthening the time spent in court for Mrs. Mrksic. So you might consider that. We now turn to a matter of very considerable concern to the Chamber, that is the estimated number of witnesses and the estimated lengths of the three Defence cases. These comments apply more significantly to the Defence cases of Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivancanin than to Mr. Radic, but they're directed to all three accused. As we understand the time estimates that have been provided, a couple of them were mathematically incorrect, but if corrected they were dealing only with the time that each counsel expected to take with their own witnesses and made no allowance for the other two Defence counsel to examine and no time for the Prosecution. If one were just to take a broad, global position and say that the other two counsel and the Prosecution together should have the same time as each Defence counsel estimated to spend with their own witness, if you added those up, we reach the middle of April next year. Now, that appears to the Chamber to be simply quite unreasonable. This trial went too slowly in the Prosecution stage. If you remember, we had to progressively impose tighter restrictions on the Prosecution to try and deal with that. We certainly do not intend to do anything to prevent the proper presentation of Defence, but we cannot comprehend that the Defence in this case could warrant evidence through until the middle of next April. That would -- with then time for final addresses and decision, we could reach almost two years to try this case. With the greatest of respect, Counsel, we suggest you need to put your thinking caps on again. Now, this is why I indicated the Chamber would reserve at the moment its position about the number of witnesses and the length, because it wants Defence counsel to think again. It's much better -- we don't know your case the way you do. It's much better that you do it rather than we attempt some sort of arbitrary dealing with it. In fairness to the accused and to your own professional skill and judgement, we would prefer that you look at the matter. It seems likely that there is some overlap in witnesses between some Defences. That firstly needs to be looked at. Secondly, there seems clearly to be overlap within particular cases. An enormous number of helicopter pilots, Mr. Mrksic, to talk about one helicopter flight, for example. We could perhaps reduce those to one or maybe, at the most, a second person who was recording official logs. That having been done, what each Defence needs to do is to look at the question: Is this a serious and significant point, a material point in defence? Not just showing some minor not-greatly-significant witness who didn't get everything right, but is this really going to advance your defence to lead this witness on a point that is really material? We would ask you to ask that question of yourselves. And then ask yourselves: If the Chamber were wanting to rule on time in a way that gave us just enough to get the essential evidence out of the witness, how long would we need with the witness? Try and impose your own time limit to avoid us wanting to do something. You will realise that it is just, it seems to the Chamber, grossly unfair to the accused for this trial to drag on to the middle of next year or even beyond, and that's where it's going at the moment unless something is done. So we would like to suggest that in the next days of this week and the next weekend there be serious attention given to that. And at an early stage of next week, we will pick it according to how witnesses are going and where it's appropriate to intervene in the flow of evidence. We want to raise again this question of the estimates of the number of witnesses and the time they are to take. And we would hope by then that each Defence will have been able to provide a revised list of witnesses with less witnesses, a revised time estimate for each witness. And we can then see whether enough has been done. If it hasn't, we're going to have to look at the Chamber taking more significant action, as the Rule provides. But we would prefer to see that being done by those who really know their own case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, I did indicate that that applies more stringently to two of the Defences, but while the Radic Defence is much shorter and restricted, I'm sure there's still some scope, Mr. Borovic, for your attention to those matters as well. When we come to witnesses, and especially at the early stage before these matters are resolved, could we indicate, particularly to Mr. Domazet but to all counsel as they deal with the witness, please ask yourself the question: Is it really important I deal with this issue or that issue? Don't worry about tedious formalities. You can accept them to be taken by the Chamber. What we are concerned about is getting to the heart of your defence, getting to the heart of the issues in this trial, and spending time on those, not wasting time on incidentals that aren't going to decide this case in the end. We have an obligation to your clients, we have an obligation to all the other accused awaiting trial, and we have an obligation to the international public to get this defence properly heard as quickly as possible; and we hope we can achieve that. Now, it's -- the issue whether it's intended that there be opening statements by counsel, I think in two of the three cases the accused made a personal statement at the beginning of the trial. I would understand that would not be thought to be repeated, but we would, of course, allow an opening statement by each counsel when they commence their case. But bear in mind, it's not a closing statement when you're revising all the evidence. Again, it can be a very pointed opening statement when you are getting to the heart of your defence. In short, get in there and try and command the attention of our minds to the critical issues, not give an expansive eloquent discussion of matters that are not going to determine this trial. A matter raised by Mr. Moore is one which we had intended to come to, that is the standard procedural orders. Is there any basis upon which any counsel would want to vary the procedural orders that we had in place for the Prosecution, the orders about provision of statements, notification of documents, things of that nature? It seemed to be working reasonably well, at least toward the end of the Prosecution case. The Prosecution had some problems early on, which gave problems for the Defence. If not, and I see no indication of any particular concern, we would propose the continuation of the existing standing procedural orders as they applied to the Prosecution to apply to the Defence, each Defence, during the course of the trial. Now, that of course requires, among other things, that there be notice of witnesses ahead of their being called. And what was in place was that notice was given two weeks ahead. Each Friday a revised notice of the next two weeks was provided, and we would have in mind that should continue. And of course that will -- at the moment the Prosecution has notice only of the first five witnesses to be called, and that will be brought up to time. And we will thereafter expect notices to be two weeks ahead, measured each Friday. Documents to be used during the evidence of a particular witness, whether by Prosecution or Defence, needs to be disclosed 24 hours in advance, if I could remind you, to the court officer for the purposes of e-court. There are some motions outstanding which will be the subject of decision in the course of this week. Some have been mentioned by some counsel already. We won't anticipate those decisions now, but we are conscious of them and counsel can be confident that decisions will be given, and that includes the Prosecution wish to interview witnesses and the notebook of P-002. Is there any further matter? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask a procedural question, since now things are turning around in this court-room, and this is a question addressed to you. Perhaps you come from a different legal system, so it's a useless question. But given the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, I would like to ask the Chamber, just so we know the position on the order of witnesses as soon as the witness is on its way, since we have a joinder on our hands. For example, I do believe that the other two Defence teams will have the right to cross-examine any of the Mrksic Defence's witnesses. What I want to know is how this Chamber feels about re-direct in a situation where, for example, Mr. Moore is examining a Mrksic Defence witness about aspects of my Defence, just by way of an example, whereas, for example, the Mrksic Defence does not feel it should clarify these issues in re-direct. In this case, will the other Defence teams have the right to address the Chamber for further clarification or would their examination be considered as some sort of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think I must say a little here to indicate what the Chamber understands to be the position. Unless there is some clear conflict of position between one Defence and another over some matter, normally we would allow each of the other two Defence teams to examine a witness. Say a witness is called by the Defence of Mrksic, if there is no conflict that's relevant to that witness, Mr. Borovic or a counsel for Mr. Radic would be able to examine the witness, not cross-examine, examine the witness, and Mr. Lukic, similarly, would be able to examine. If there's a point where the Defences are in conflict, that would become a right to cross-examine the witness. But you could examine further. The Prosecution has a right to cross-examine at large on relevant matters. Normally, the only re-examination would be that of counsel for Mr. Mrksic. If some very unusual situation arose that was not able to be resolved between Defence counsel in time for that re-examination, a motion might be made specially for leave to re-examine, but that will be unusual. So normally, only the counsel calling the witness would re-examine. You didn't mention one matter which I think we have mentioned before but I will mention again. Normally if an accused is to be called as a witness, he would be called as the first witness. It's not an inviable rule. There may be circumstances that justifies something different, but if the accused is not the first person called and is left, for example, until last, immediately the weight to be attached to that accused's evidence can suffer because it appears that he is then able to adjust his evidence to all the witnesses that have been called before, whereas if he comes and gives his evidence first, there can be no such suspicions about his evidence. Has that dealt with your concerns, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very much so, Your Honour. You have understood my query fully, and your answer definitely sheds light on my dilemma. I can also inform you that even prior to what you have just said Mr. Sljivancanin's position was that he would be the first witness to appear. Before our Defence case really gets off the ground, we shall be presenting some sort of an opening statement. Given our position in these proceedings, it will be much closer to a closing argument than anything else, but we shall try to fully comply with your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And even with our best hopes, that will be a little way away; it won't be happening very shortly. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our position is the same as Mr. Sljivancanin's position. We also believe that regardless of the order indicated on the 65 ter list, Miroslav Radic should be the first to appear in order to state his case as a witness, and we shall also be presenting a brief opening statement at the beginning of our case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, you did foreshadow the possibility that we might sit only four days a week. Could I indicate that for the reasons which we've already indicated, unless there's some dramatic revision in the list of witnesses and the time estimates, that is not going to be possible. So if Mr. Vasic is ever in a position where he needs a day off, you will have to cover fully on that day. We take it, Mr. Domazet, that you have a witness ready for Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first things first. We shall do our best; there's no doubt about that. I expect that we shall be able to curtail our witness list in terms of how many witnesses there are and also in terms of how long individual witnesses will take. We shall do whatever we can to take less time for all of this. As for our first witness, I truly don't know what the situation is with our first witness, since this used to be a witness on the OTP's 65 ter list, P-019, a protected witness from that list, who refused for the OTP to submit his information to us so that we may get in touch. The Chamber has reacted in a speedy fashion by issuing a subpoena. Nonetheless, to this very day, I still don't know whether this witness will in fact be appearing. I would also like to have a word with the witness before he appears. The situation being what it is, I truly don't know how we stand on that and I'm not sure how far we got. It is my intention to personally examine this witness in order to ease Mr. Vasic back into this trial. By all means, it would be exceptionally important for the Mrksic Defence if we could start on Monday, provided the witness is able to appear earlier, which we don't know, because we would start with Mr. Vasic, and then there would be a brief opening statement by the lead counsel, as is normally done. If that should not be possible, I will do my best to start before Monday, provided we have the witness in The Hague, and even should I not be able to see the witness beforehand and talk to him, although I still hope and believe that this would be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Domazet, and we support you in your efforts. We did send a message to you, I believe, that should there be a problem with the witness you intend to be your first, that you have your next witness available. That has been arranged, has it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour, I received that message, and I duly responded that we would be doing our best. It is, however, exceptionally difficult. We are facing a great deal of difficulty organising our witnesses, and as we speak Mr. Vasic is working on this. There are problems involving their passports, their visas, their arrival. I think it is impossible to expect that any of the witnesses -- of the four witnesses, foreseen for the following week, will be here this week. If P-019, the first witness on our list, who is a protected witness, is unable to make it this week, then it is not very likely that any other witnesses would be appearing. I am truly sorry, but this seems to be the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, we don't find that very satisfactory. We do expect that there will be a witness to give evidence on Wednesday. Do I make that clear? Very well. We appear then -- Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- you did ask whether there were any matters to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To try and lighten the court atmosphere a little, can I just deal with my learned friend Mr. Lukic's ability to dust table-tops and Hoover carpets because his housekeeping is not quite as we would hope. If Your Honour looks at the list, you will see that the defendant Mr. Sljivancanin has managed a summary, I think, of 18 lines, which, given the time estimate of between 15 and 20, is one line per hour. We would ask and I think we have indicated that we would wish to have, please, a proper and appropriate summary indicating facts from that particular defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please discuss that with Mr. Lukic. I think at the moment his good housekeeping seal of approval stands very much higher than was possible at this stage of the Prosecution case, Mr. Moore, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We shall see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- tread carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with one or two other matters? Your Honour has dealt with whether in actual fact we are going to have a witness this week. Secondly, in relation to the application to interview or speak to a witness, a Defence witness, we rely clearly on the authorities that Your Honours add, namely paragraph 15, that there is no property in evidence. And then the fourth and final point, Your Honour did say that documents that were to be used by witnesses, that that should be 24 hours in advance. We would seek that that be 48 hours in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I hope I mentioned that was for the e-court for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For opposing counsel it was 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I should have said more. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So it is 48 hours for notice in relation to the documentation; 24 hours for e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's the least time that e-court needs. They would appreciate 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a good time for me to raise another housekeeping matter, but I believe this should be done in private session. It's not in reference to what Mr. Moore has just been saying, but it's certainly something that I wish to advise the Chamber of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. May we thank counsel for their attendance, and we need now to adjourn until Wednesday at 2.15. We are in another court-room, I believe the small one. We adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: adjourned at 3.49 p.m. 22 23 24 25
